summary: This project proposes a hypothetical human excursion to the ancient delta of Jezero Crater, Mars, together with a digital interface designed to support astronauts before, during and after the mission. The scientific goal is to collect data on the geological structures of the former delta in the hope of identifying potential biosignatures. The technological answer is a smart helmet whose visor displays a live, region-specific map and acts as a mission companion from A to Z: it prepares the route, monitors the environment and the astronaut’s physiology, guides scientific observations and records every relevant datum for post-mission analysis. Because no human has yet walked on Mars, all astronaut-related values are plausible hypotheses anchored as far as possible in existing scientific data, and are explicitly identified as such.
details:
I) Context

Why Jezero Crater ? This project addresses an unprecedented exploration mission: the conquest of the red planet. On a planet as large as Mars, the first question is where to go. We chose Jezero Crater (approximately 18.41° N, 77.69° E) for its scientific and geological interest: the crater hosted a lake, and life could therefore have developed there. Jezero has already been explored by rovers, and the Perseverance rover has just found, in October 2026, an extremely promising mineral rock in the crater. Satellite imagery further reveals the structure of this ancient water system. On the western side of our study area, what appears to be a dried-up riverbed is clearly visible. Higher up in the imagery, a zone corresponds to the mouth of this ancient river as it entered the crater, which was therefore filled by a lake. The river most likely ended in a delta.

Why astronauts ? Rovers are slow, limited in their movements, and cannot reach the most interesting places. This is why astronauts are needed. We chose the location of a base, which would be the starting point of every mission, and we propose to work in the deltaic zone.

II) Scientific Background

On Earth, a delta forms where a river flows into a large body of water and splits into multiple branches called distributaries. It is a zone of intense sedimentary deposition. The river carries rock fragments, and on reaching the delta the water loses speed. The transported particles then settle on the bed, the coarsest first and then the finest. If Earth deltas are taken as a guide, the same sedimentary arrangement should be found at Jezero. The zone we wish to explore lies at the very end of the delta plain, at the foot of the sediment deposits coming from the shoreline. According to the model proposed by NASA, this area was submerged for a long time. We therefore expect deposits made of very fine particles, and potentially microfossils such as algae or the exoskeletons of microorganisms. This expectation is consistent with the fact that deltas are areas of very high biological proliferation, for microorganisms as well as larger organisms (the Nile delta is one example). Studying this zone would therefore bring two kinds of information. The sedimentation recorded in the former lake gives valuable information on the planet’s ancient climates. The possible presence of fossils would provide evidence of ancient forms of life.

III) Mission Scenario and methodology

The excursion we planned is purely hypothetical. Its aim is to collect data on the geological structures of the ancient delta, in the hope of finding potential biosignatures. To define it, we reviewed the available resources to decide where a trajectory would be most relevant, under three constraints. The trajectory had to be short enough for the astronauts never to be too far from the imagined base in the event of a solar storm. It also had to pass near a flat surface where the base spaceship could land, and near interesting geological structures. Once these conditions had been examined, we drew three different trajectories in the same area. They are more or less feasible depending on the time available and the weather conditions. We then prompted Gemini and Copilot, integrated in VS Code, to generate a hyperlocalized map of the three intended trajectories. Along these trajectories, the astronauts can explore three areas, each corresponding to a stop for experiments: the cliff, the sloping alluvial plain, and the slopes of the talus north of the trajectory. The three trajectories were imagined around these three stops.

IV) Excursion Plan : 3 Stops

The excursion heads towards the zone where carbonates occur, the most likely place to find signs of life. Since the astronauts are working on the delta, the grain size of the sediments should normally decrease with distance from the shoreline, i.e. towards the base. Besides carbonates, the astronauts look for stromatolites, ripples and alluvial terraces, which reveal potential variations in water level and must be photographed. They also search the recesses of the deposits for traces of microorganisms. Evaporites would be informative too, but they probably lie at depth and may not be observable. 

The first stop is a cliff about 20 m high, reached over 200 m of walking during which the astronauts also photograph, observe and sample. They examine the outcrop for anomalies that could be biomarkers, and look along the whole route for crevasses, ice and unusual outcrops. Drilling here gives access to very old fluvio-lacustrine sediments, but it must be deep enough to avoid sampling only sand blown in by sandstorms. The bottomsets and foresets are the priority targets, as they are the most interesting scientifically. If they are easily accessible, the astronauts sample horizontally in the sedimentary layers, at depth to escape surface erosion and if possible at different altitudes. If access is difficult (a manipulation lasting more than one hour), they photograph the layers and record the precise location for a future mission. Since this stop is very exposed, with winds from the east and south-east and no visible shelter on satellite maps, it is best carried out when there is no wind. 

The second stop lies 300 m away, at the foot of the talus, about 15 minutes’ walk given the extra loads the astronauts may carry. They look for isolated places that have been little degraded or eroded. They also look for “leopard skin” patterns. A sample taken by Perseverance near our site shows small black dots that may be due to fossilized microbial activity. Two minerals are suspected inside them, vivianite and greigite, both iron-rich and, on Earth, indicators of the decomposition of organic matter. Wherever such structures appear, the astronauts also sample the surrounding rock that lacks them. This comparison shows whether the dots could instead result from an abiotic reaction such as metamorphism. 

The third stop is an ancient shoreline, where the astronauts look for stromatolites and for any other formation suggesting biological activity. On Earth, stromatolites consist of alternating layers of fossilized cyanobacteria and calcium carbonate. They could also be present at the cliff, but here, near this “beach”, they would most likely be buried. 

Sampling and measurement protocol (hypothetical guidelines) : Wherever possible, the astronauts dig and sample in places sheltered from the wind, and therefore from erosion, such as crevasses, small corridors and meanders. Because dust and sand will probably cover the structures of interest, the surface must be scraped and sampled at the slightest doubt. Several samples are always taken at the same place to ensure representativeness, and fragments need not be larger than a fist. Each sample is photographed in its context, especially when it comes from an outcrop, which places it in its environment and allows geographic correlation of data. Several photographs are taken at different zoom levels, always with the location and shooting direction, and if possible with an instrument as a scale. Assuming there is no communication with the rear base, the precise coordinates are also written on the bag that receives the sample. Contamination must be avoided before and after the expedition: sterility is ensured when preparing the equipment (bags, pliers, shovels), and the samples are stored properly on return. The analysis continues after the mission, through laboratory study of the minerals and the search for biosignatures, notably isotopic ratios. 

V) The Smart-Helmet Interface

The astronauts will not go on this mission alone: our technology supports them before, during and after every excursion. It works through a smart helmet that displays the map directly on the visor. It is not just a map but a mission companion from A to Z. The idea came from fields that face similar challenges on Earth, such as hiking, aviation and mountain rescue plans. We took the best of each and adapted it to Mars.

In our scenario, the astronaut operates from a base in the chosen region, and the base and the helmet exchange data continuously. The base measures the conditions of the region and transmits them live. The helmet, being connected, collects the astronaut’s health information itself, and also sees, measures and reports back. The verdict on a route comes from crossing the two: the conditions of the region and the state of the astronaut. The exchange starts before departure, because the mission does not begin when the astronauts leave the base. To prepare them, the interface takes into account the route, the ground, the timings, the light, the environment, the suit, the astronaut’s health and the scientific purposes.

The interface integrates five families of criteria. Route and terrain covers the hyperlocal map, distance, elevation change, slope, rocks, the return to the habitat and the comparison of two routes. Time and light covers soil and local time, sunrise and sunset, the turn-back deadline and the duration of the excursion. Environment covers temperature and cold, dust, wind, radiation and the solar storm alert. Suit and physiology covers available O₂, physical effort, fatigue, travel speed and suit weight. Science covers the objective of the stop, geology, minerals, the sample list and images.

Everything displayed on the visor (local information, health information, route information, vision layers and objectives) obeys three principles, without exception. First, everything is live. Every value updates continuously, without user action, and reflects the real situation at that instant. Local information evolves with time, health information with effort, and route information is recalculated continuously. The traffic-light verdict is dynamic, alerts are instantaneous and the vision layers (the five buttons) are refreshed. Emergency mode is computed on demand, instantly. Second, everything is specialized for the chosen region: the relief, terrain and rock, local climate, radiation, rhythm of the Sun, objectives, points of interest and starting base are all specific to it. Third, everything is consistent with the routes and distances described. Displayed distances are exactly those of the route tab, travel times derive from them, and the proposed routes are those of the route tab. Health information is linked to the routes, so the green, orange or red verdict follows logically from them. The turn-back time and the maximum distance are deduced from the reserves, emergency mode respects the same distances, and the objective cards are aligned with the route.

Since Mars is extreme, action windows must be calculated carefully. Each indicator has green, orange and red thresholds that show whether the mission is feasible at a given moment T. In practice, the interface chooses the best route from the parameters, schedules it according to time and conditions, and offers a simulation of the route for training and preparation.

Once the astronauts are outside, the interface stays with them and has three roles. It keeps them safe: it monitors weather and health indicators in real time, sends alerts when needed and lets them turn back at any moment with an emergency button. It keeps the mission on track: it follows progress in time and distance, and the astronaut can switch between vision layers to help with movement and observation. It helps them reach their scientific goals: the astronaut sees the mission objective and the number of stops, and for each stop the interface gives its geology, the minerals to look for and a list of observations and samples. As an example of safety information, the astronaut stays less than 1.5 km from the base at all times. This protects against solar storms, which are very hard to predict and leave only 30 to 90 minutes to regain the base once detected.

As precursors on Mars, every piece of data is precious, so the interface records the relevant indicators live. As soon as the astronaut validates a route, the system records everything automatically, without manual intervention, until the end of the mission. The aim is not only to pilot the mission but to keep a complete trace that can be analyzed afterwards. The route, technical data, events, decisions and crew data are all recorded, each with a precise date and time so that the exact chronology can be reconstructed. This record allows a precise report to be produced, conclusions to be drawn, errors to be learned from and new missions to be prepared.

VI) Assumptions and Limitations

No human mission to Mars has yet taken place, and no inhabited base exists there. We therefore have no real data from astronauts walking on Mars. We build hypotheses, i.e. plausible values and behaviors, anchored as far as possible in existing scientific data. Our project is based on the data we could find in the Space Apps resources. A number of choices were made (location of the base, length and stops of the journey, structures requiring attention) that are mostly hypothetical and would require further investigation before humans were sent on a mission to Mars. The sampling instructions, thresholds and distances presented here are likewise hypothetical.

VII) Conclusion

The ancient delta of Jezero Crater combines a past lake, fine sedimentary deposits and the potential for preserved biosignatures, yet its most interesting places lie beyond the reach of rovers. Our project answers this limit with a short-range, safety-conscious excursion supported by a connected helmet, which turns live conditions at the base and the astronaut’s physiological state into a single green, orange or red verdict. Its intended impact is to make the first human excursions on Mars safer and better prepared, and to leave future missions a documented basis to build on. Although the values we propose remain hypotheses, they offer a coherent framework that future missions could test, refine and adapt to other sites on Mars.
